```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
post <- dirname(normalizePath(knitr::current_input(dir=TRUE),mustWork=TRUE))
folder <- file.path(post,"data","aggregate")
est <- read.csv(file.path(folder,"estimates.csv"))
diffs <- read.csv(file.path(folder,"paired_differences.csv"))
flow <- read.csv(file.path(folder,"sample_flow.csv"))

stopifnot(nrow(est)==4,all(tolower(checks$passed)=="true"))
```

**Does measuring the same sons’ incomes earlier in adulthood give a lower intergenerational income elasticity (IGE)?** IGE measures how strongly higher parental income is associated with higher adult-child income. Using real PSID records and SQL within Python, we match fathers and sons and compare income windows while holding pairs fixed.

## 1. Prepare the records

The inputs are the **2023 Parent Identification File**, its matching **1968–2023 Individual File**, and nine annual Family Files. Here, “parent income” means total money income of the father's family; “child income” means the adult son's own family income. Neither is individual wages.

Download the files listed in the [README](README.md) into `data/raw/`. In a terminal, open this post’s directory and install dependencies:

```bash
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
```

Next, create a new SQLite database:

```bash
python scripts/prepare_psid_linkage.py --raw data/raw --db data/private/psid.sqlite --out data/aggregate
```

This script parses official fixed-width records, checks identifiers, and stores parent–child links in SQLite. Skip this command if `data/private/psid.sqlite` already exists; it refuses to overwrite the database.

Then load the annual family incomes and run the analysis:

```bash
python scripts/psid_analysis.py --raw data/raw --db data/private/psid.sqlite --out data/aggregate --cpi data/aggregate/cpi_annual.csv
```

This script converts income to **1996 dollars** using CPI-U, selects the sample, constructs income measures, and estimates IGEs. Summaries go to `data/aggregate/`; microdata remain local.

Run the following blocks in order, in one Python session from this directory.

## 2. Match people using two-part identifiers

Before comparing incomes, we need to know whose father we are measuring. An adult son may live elsewhere, so sharing a current household is not a reliable matching rule. PSID’s parent-identification table supplies the relationship; the individual table lets us check both people.

The [PSID guide, Section 8.14.2](https://psidonline.isr.umich.edu/data/Documentation/UserGuide2019.pdf), identifies each person using **1968 Family Interview Number (`ER30001`) and Person Number (`ER30002`) together**. Our tables call these `fid` and `pnum`. First, open the prepared database:

```python
import sqlite3

con = sqlite3.connect("data/private/psid.sqlite")
```

For each relationship in `parent_ids`, look up the child in `persons` as `c`, then the father as `p`. Each `JOIN` matches both identifiers. A pair remains only if both lookups succeed:

```python
con.execute("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS temp.tutorial_pairs")
con.execute("""
CREATE TEMP TABLE tutorial_pairs AS
SELECT r.child_fid, r.child_pnum,
       r.father_fid AS parent_fid, r.father_pnum AS parent_pnum
FROM parent_ids r
JOIN persons c ON c.fid=r.child_fid AND c.pnum=r.child_pnum
JOIN persons p ON p.fid=r.father_fid AND p.pnum=r.father_pnum
WHERE r.father_fid>0 AND r.father_pnum BETWEEN 1 AND 995;
""")
```

`SELECT` keeps the identifiers, `AS` renames the father columns, and `WHERE` filters father identifiers. Check the resulting number of links:

```python
n_pairs = con.execute(
    "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM tutorial_pairs"
).fetchone()[0]
print(f"Recorded father–child links: {n_pairs:,}")
assert n_pairs == 29218
```

This release produces **29,218 child–father links**; siblings can share a father. This is a relationship lookup, not yet the income-analysis sample or independent verification of biological fatherhood. Next, we select sons with the income histories needed for the comparison.

## 3. Construct both generations' incomes

Keep the pairs fixed to compare income windows. Select sons born in **1955–1959** without conflicting birth-year reports; require fathers to respond as heads in 1969–1971, aged 25–65, and sons as heads in 1985–1987 and 1995–1997:

```python
con.executescript("""
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS psid_candidates;
CREATE TABLE psid_candidates AS
SELECT l.*, c.birth_year,
 (SELECT age FROM waves w WHERE w.fid=l.parent_fid AND w.pnum=l.parent_pnum AND year=1970) AS parent_age_1970,
 (SELECT age FROM waves w WHERE w.fid=l.child_fid AND w.pnum=l.child_pnum AND year=1986) AS child_age_1986,
 (SELECT age FROM waves w WHERE w.fid=l.child_fid AND w.pnum=l.child_pnum AND year=1996) AS child_age_1996
FROM tutorial_pairs l JOIN persons c ON c.fid=l.child_fid AND c.pnum=l.child_pnum
WHERE c.sex=1 AND c.birth_year BETWEEN 1955 AND 1959 AND c.birth_discrepancy=0
 AND (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM waves w WHERE w.fid=l.parent_fid AND w.pnum=l.parent_pnum
      AND year IN (1969,1970,1971) AND relation=1 AND age BETWEEN 25 AND 65)=3
 AND (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM waves w WHERE w.fid=l.child_fid AND w.pnum=l.child_pnum
      AND year IN (1985,1986,1987,1995,1996,1997) AND relation=10)=6;
""")
```

For these 197 pairs, attach household income by **survey year and annual family ID**. Prepared `waves` records identify responding members; headship codes are 1 early, 10 later:

```python
con.executescript("""
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS psid_income;
CREATE TABLE psid_income AS
SELECT w.fid,w.pnum,w.year,f.real_income,
 CASE WHEN w.year BETWEEN 1969 AND 1971 THEN 'parent'
      WHEN w.year BETWEEN 1985 AND 1987 THEN 'early' ELSE 'mid' END AS window
FROM waves w JOIN psid_family_income f ON f.wave=w.year AND f.family=w.family
WHERE f.valid=1 AND ((w.year BETWEEN 1969 AND 1971 AND w.relation=1)
 OR (w.year IN (1985,1986,1987,1995,1996,1997) AND w.relation=10));
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX psid_income_key ON psid_income(fid,pnum,year);
""")
```

Income is in 1996 dollars; `valid` excludes nonpositive, one-dollar bottom-coded, upper-coded, and sentinel values. Previous-year reporting gives windows **1968–1970, 1984–1986, 1994–1996**. Prevent duplicate person-years with a unique index, then summarize:

```python
con.executescript("""
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS psid_measures;
CREATE TABLE psid_measures AS
SELECT fid,pnum,window,AVG(real_income) AS mean_income,
 MAX(CASE WHEN year IN (1970,1986,1996) THEN real_income END) AS single_income,
 COUNT(*) AS n_valid
FROM psid_income GROUP BY fid,pnum,window HAVING COUNT(*)=3;
""")
```

`GROUP BY` groups each person’s window; `AVG` averages income levels. `MAX(CASE...)` retrieves the middle year, not the highest income. `HAVING` requires three valid years. Join summaries before comparing measures:

```python
con.executescript("""
DROP TABLE IF EXISTS psid_matched;
CREATE TABLE psid_matched AS
SELECT k.child_fid,k.child_pnum,k.parent_fid,k.parent_pnum,k.birth_year,
 k.parent_age_1970,k.child_age_1986,k.child_age_1996,
 p.single_income AS p_single,p.mean_income AS p_mean,
 e.single_income AS c_early_single,e.mean_income AS c_early_mean,
 m.single_income AS c_mid_single,m.mean_income AS c_mid_mean
FROM psid_candidates k
JOIN psid_measures p ON p.fid=k.parent_fid AND p.pnum=k.parent_pnum AND p.window='parent'
JOIN psid_measures e ON e.fid=k.child_fid AND e.pnum=k.child_pnum AND e.window='early'
JOIN psid_measures m ON m.fid=k.child_fid AND m.pnum=k.child_pnum AND m.window='mid';
""")
```

Summarizing first avoids multiplying annual records. Check son uniqueness and father counts:

```python
n_pairs = con.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM psid_matched").fetchone()[0]
n_sons = con.execute("""
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (
 SELECT DISTINCT child_fid,child_pnum FROM psid_matched
);
""").fetchone()[0]
n_fathers = con.execute("""
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (
 SELECT DISTINCT parent_fid,parent_pnum FROM psid_matched
);
""").fetchone()[0]
assert n_pairs == n_sons == 191
assert n_fathers == 170
print(f"Complete sample: {n_sons} sons, {n_fathers} fathers")
```

Part 4 uses these **191 sons and 170 fathers** throughout; sample membership stays fixed.

## 4. Estimate the IGE on the same pairs

Estimate the intergenerational elasticity (IGE) with a log-income regression:

$$
\log(Y_i^{son})=\alpha+\beta\log(Y_i^{father})+u_i.
$$

$\beta$ is the IGE: 0.5 associates 10% higher parental income with approximately 5% higher son income, without implying causation. Take the **log of mean real income** for averages:

```python
import numpy as np

specs = [("Early single","p_single","c_early_single"),
         ("Midlife single","p_single","c_mid_single"),
         ("Early average","p_mean","c_early_mean"),
         ("Midlife average","p_mean","c_mid_mean")]
```

For each specification, retrieve incomes, take logs, and estimate a slope with an intercept:

```python
for label, px, cy in specs:  # fixed column names, not user input
    rows = con.execute(f"SELECT {px},{cy} FROM psid_matched").fetchall()
    x,y = np.log(np.asarray(rows,dtype=float)).T
    X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(x)),x])
    beta = np.linalg.lstsq(X,y,rcond=None)[0][1]
    print(f"{label}: n={len(x)}, IGE={beta:.3f}")
con.close()
```

These are point estimates. The full script supplies percentile intervals from 500 father-cluster bootstrap samples, keeping siblings together.

```{r}
#| label: results-table
tab <- data.frame(Measurement=c("Single year: father 1969 / son 1985", "Single year: father 1969 / son 1995", "Three-year means: father 1968-1970 / son 1984-1986", "Three-year means: father 1968-1970 / son 1994-1996"),IGE=fmt(est$ige),
                  `95% interval`=paste0("[",fmt(est$ci_low),", ",fmt(est$ci_high),"]"),check.names=FALSE)
knitr::kable(tab,caption="IGE estimates for the same 191 father-son pairs. Intervals are 95% percentile bootstrap intervals.")
```

## 5. Interpret timing and averaging separately

With the father’s 1969 income held fixed, the single-year IGE is **`r fmt(est$ige[1])`** for sons’ earlier incomes and **`r fmt(est$ige[2])`** later. Mean interview ages are about 29 and 38. The paired difference interval, [`r fmt(diffs$ci_low[1])`, `r fmt(diffs$ci_high[1])`], includes zero. This does not establish a positive difference or an age effect: calendar year changes too, and household composition is not fixed.

**Life-cycle bias** concerns how income at a particular age represents long-run status ([Haider and Solon](https://cpi.stanford.edu/_media/pdf/Reference%20Media/Haider%20and%20Solon_2006_Lifecourse%2C%20Family%2C%20and%20Demography.pdf)). Suppose early log income equals half of long-run log income plus noise uncorrelated with accurately measured parental long-run log income. Its slope would be half the long-run IGE—a conditional illustration, not our estimated bias.

Averaging **both generations’** incomes gives **`r fmt(est$ige[4])`** in the later window, versus **`r fmt(est$ige[2])`** using single years. The paired difference interval, [`r fmt(diffs$ci_low[2])`, `r fmt(diffs$ci_high[2])`], also includes zero. Averages can smooth temporary fluctuations ([measurement rationale](https://www.chicagofed.org/research/content-areas/mobility/intergenerational-economic-mobility)); that reduction is not measured here. Averaging does not automatically remove age-related measurement problems or guarantee greater accuracy.

## Takeaway

For these same 191 sons, earlier measurement gives lower estimated persistence: **`r fmt(est$ige[1])` versus `r fmt(est$ige[2])`**. The difference interval includes zero, however, and age cannot be separated from calendar year. Averaging can smooth temporary fluctuations; our results do not establish greater accuracy or eliminate life-cycle bias. The practical lesson: match both identifiers, aggregate before joining generations, and compare fixed samples. These selected, unweighted estimates are not national results.

[PSID linkage documentation](https://psidonline.isr.umich.edu/documents/psid/intro/pid23intro.pdf), [CPI source](https://www.minneapolisfed.org/about-us/monetary-policy/inflation-calculator/consumer-price-index-1913-), [life-cycle measurement research](https://www.nber.org/papers/w11943), and [complete replication instructions](README.md).
